apps.name: Actual Budget
pitfalls: The server password is not the optional budget end-to-end encryption password; the latter cannot be recovered if lost.
External bank synchronization can introduce third-party credentials and terms.
security: Keep financial data private, protect the server password, and verify backups with an isolated restore.

apps.name: AdGuard Home
pitfalls: DNS, DHCP, and bootstrap ports can conflict with host services.
security: Keep administration private; publishing DNS port 53 and changing LAN or host DNS require a separate owner-approved cutover with fallback DNS.

apps.name: ArchiveTeam Warrior
pitfalls: It runs externally assigned archival workloads and is not a backup or personal web archive.
The exact publisher digest is a valid immutable image pin; the version label 20260917.01 is not a registry tag and must not be fabricated as one. The verified image is linux/amd64 only.

Startup environment variables seed config.json only when it cannot be loaded; later restarts can ignore changed values. A corrupt config can trigger reseeding, so recovery is not a credential-rotation contract. A reachable UI or live container does not prove an approved project is running or uploads have completed.

HTTP_USERNAME and HTTP_PASSWORD protect the control interface with HTTP authentication; they do not create a local administrator account or durable API key. No API-key provisioning contract was established.

Read-only OCI inspection on 2026-10-03 verified immutable manifest/config, compressed layer SHA-256, and later-layer overlays/whiteouts. run-warrior3 imports seesaw.script.run_warrior; final library-copy layer direct_url.json pins seesaw bb6673d27a8717e13efe5d7deb3628349cd08585 and six runtime source files byte-match that revision. Earlier reviewed seesaw 699b0d2 is not the installed revision. The unpinned clone's installed warrior-code2 Git ref is 465aa2223a9d6d863f3e8ff173eaf8bfb5fbd0d5; labels alone would not establish either dependency.

The publisher healthcheck reads /index.html on port 8001; it proves only that the web frontend responds. Projects and seeded config.json live in the container's Warrior projects directory; retain only reviewed project-owned storage, and do not mistake temporary downloads for an archive or backup.

The shared recipe supports only explicitly selected idle mode: nickname, selected_project=none, concurrency=1, HQ registration/update traffic, CPU 1 and memory 512 MiB. The owner requires private writable UID-1000 configuration and exact resume validation before controlled start. No disk quota, HQ bandwidth cap or network destination firewall is implemented. Archival workload approval and acceptance remain separate and unsupported; idle readiness is not zero external work.

The current manual-job contract permits fixed publisher version probes only for restic, Borgmatic and Renovate. No pinned canonical Warrior probe with verified image provenance was established; overriding its entrypoint with an arbitrary no-op would neither verify its runner nor configure the cataloged archival workload.
security: The container actively downloads and uploads Archive Team work; require explicit consent to the selected project, outbound traffic, resource use, and destination policy before start.

SELECTED_PROJECT=none is not an offline bootstrap: the upstream runner registers and sends updates to Warrior HQ during startup. Approve those external writes separately, or establish and verify an inert bootstrap with fail-closed egress before normal shared apply.

Keep the port 8001 web control interface private. Configure its documented HTTP_USERNAME and HTTP_PASSWORD together before exposing it to other users; do not assume it has an administrator account by default.
Do not include the recommended Watchtower Docker-socket mount in a shared Compose project. Review image updates as a separate scoped action.

apps.name: Aria2
pitfalls: An exposed RPC listener can permit arbitrary downloads and filesystem writes within its process authority.
aria2c listens only on loopback by default; a container RPC listener needs an explicit reachability decision and separate private host binding.
aria2 has no username account; its RPC token is the control credential, not an administrator password.
The third-party image's publisher startup passes RPC_HASH in argv and logs a generated secret; do not use it unchanged or bypass the shared recipe's secret boundary.

The publisher Dockerfile uses root, but aria2 RPC on port 6800 needs no privileged mode, Docker socket, host networking, or host-root mount. A non-root override still needs pinned image and writable-storage evidence.

Authenticated aria2.getVersion is a read-only control-token check; system.listMethods is allowed without a token and cannot prove authentication. Downloads, session persistence, and VPN safety need separate acceptance.
security: Keep JSON-RPC on a private route and require --rpc-secret before enabling remote control.
Keep the RPC token out of process arguments, logs, Compose manifests, and ordinary reports.

apps.name: Audiobookshelf
pitfalls: File ownership, metadata matching, and database plus media backup must be planned together.
security: Protect accounts, listening history, library metadata, and remote access.

apps.name: Authelia
pitfalls: Forward-auth headers and application trust boundaries need per-app testing.

The file authentication backend requires a writable hashed user database. The mutable owner prepares it exclusively and verifies identity/hash on resume; password resets or changed users stop rather than reseed.

Official Compose examples require configuration.yml and readable secret files. Authelia requires a user-chosen cookie domain and HTTPS Authelia URL; localhost is explicitly invalid. Access rules, notifier, and proxy wiring need approval for the actual deployment. No public route or identity-provider key can be inferred from a loopback Compose port.

The file backend creates login users, not a separate administrator API token. Generated login credentials need hash verification, authenticated owner readback, and restart persistence before readiness; a running authentication portal is insufficient.

The non-root numeric host user bypasses the pinned entrypoint's root-only /config chown. Immutable configuration, writable users, and private SQLite/notifier state use separate mount paths. Source evidence is not live image acceptance.

An applied private HTTPS route alone cannot bootstrap Authelia: an eligible non-localhost cookie domain, matching HTTPS authelia_url, writable hashed user database, and approved protected application target are required. Verify intended-client DNS/trust, login identity, forward-auth denial and allow behavior, and persistence separately; never relax cookie-domain validation to make the portal start.
security: Protect file-based session, storage, and reset-password secrets and preserve a recovery route.
Treat proxy trust, session cookie domains, and protected application routes as separately approved ingress decisions.

apps.name: Authentik
pitfalls: A failed IdP change can lock users out of every protected service.
The official Compose example mounts the Docker socket for automatic outpost management; omit it and manage outposts separately unless a reviewed privilege boundary is approved.
security: Keep a tested break-glass administrator and protect signing material.

apps.name: Bazarr
pitfalls: Mount the same selected media root at /data as Sonarr and Radarr; subtitles require write access to media files.
Compose start alone does not establish login or API access; the shared adapter must verify both against the exact private origin.
The shared adapter does not configure Sonarr, Radarr, subtitle providers, or download and subtitle-path acceptance.
security: Keep the web UI private; the shared first-run adapter configures Basic authentication, but any wider access needs separate review.
Store provider and Arr credentials outside catalog and preferences.

apps.name: Beszel
pitfalls: Monitoring can gain host-level visibility beyond ordinary app scope.
The hub alone has no machine metrics; an agent needs separate privilege and network review.

The pinned first-run HTTP route creates separate Hub admin and PocketBase superuser accounts. Shared setup uses fixed admin@example.test; change that identity through a separately reviewed workflow, not an unbound runtime input.
Beszel's universal token is an agent enrollment credential, not a general REST API key; this setup does not create or export it.
security: Treat Docker socket or host-agent access as explicit privilege.

apps.name: BookStack
pitfalls: Database and uploaded files must be backed up consistently.

The first-admin adapter uses bookstack:create-admin --initial --generate-password, capturing only its success stdout into the owner-only password file. If the database changes but that file is not saved, the result is ambiguous: never rerun the initial command or present the pre-generated placeholder as a working credential; recover through a separately approved private route.

The pinned v26.05.3 own-account form creates one API token inheriting the saved administrator's permissions, expiring 2099-01-01. Shared setup separately approves creation and the once-returned secret read, privately saves Token ID:Secret, and verifies the exact owner through the API. Interrupted creation or missing secret output requires inspection, never another token. No database extraction is used; live login, content, restart, and restore acceptance remain unverified.
security: The packaged container starts with publicly known admin@admin.com/password credentials; replace them before any exposure.
Keep APP_URL fixed to the reviewed origin and review registration, public access, roles, attachments, and SSO before exposure.

apps.name: Borgmatic
pitfalls: The publisher documents daily scheduling by default and CRON=false to disable it; do not start a backup schedule before separate source, destination, and write approval.
The recipe's managed source and repository folders are empty staging placeholders, not selected production data or an independent off-host copy.
Hooks must fail closed when a database dump or quiesce step fails; a successful archive still requires an isolated restore drill.
security: Protect the Borg repository passphrase, keyfiles, and any remote SSH key outside ordinary reports and logs.
Select backup sources and a repository destination only after their exact ownership is known; do not mount the Docker socket by default.

apps.name: Caddy
pitfalls: ACME challenge modes have different port and DNS-secret requirements.

The bundled recipe exposes only readiness and exact GET /reverse_proxy/upstreams on private port 2015; writable admin stays on container loopback. Upstream statistics do not prove application ingress, and changing a saved recipe requires an explicitly reviewed transition.
security: Make Caddy the sole approved owner of selected ingress ports.

apps.name: Cloudflare Tunnel
pitfalls: Connector readiness can be checked at its local metrics /ready endpoint, but this does not prove a route is private or authenticated; a published application route can make its origin Internet-accessible.
Token-file ingestion is available from cloudflared 2025.4.0 onward. Importing a token is not route approval, and no local administrator or generated API key should be fabricated for this connector.

Remote configuration readback uses GET /accounts/{account_id}/cfd_tunnel/{tunnel_id}/configurations with a separately scoped Cloudflare API credential. The connector token alone is not the generic setup engine's cloud-account API credential or an exact route approval.
Local tunnel ingress validate and ingress rule commands check configuration without enrollment or route changes; they do not inspect remotely managed routes or verify origin delivery.

The pinned native tunnel --metrics 127.0.0.1:2000 ready command checks the container-private readiness endpoint without shell/curl or a published metrics port. It does not establish tunnel identity, mounted credential readability, DNS/auth policy, selected-origin delivery or client acceptance.

Pinned tunnel diag requires an existing local metrics instance, collects configuration even when optional logs and metrics are disabled, and can exit successfully with no instance or diagnostic failures. Neither its exit status nor its report is safe generic setup acceptance.
security: A remotely managed tunnel needs an existing Cloudflare-issued token. Use the bounded owner-supplied mode-0600 secret-file import and TUNNEL_TOKEN_FILE if a separately approved connector workflow is added; generated random privateFiles cannot substitute for the token. Never put it in catalog data, argv, plans, or logs.

Before starting the connector, inspect existing remotely managed routes and obtain a separate public-exposure approval covering the exact route, DNS, TLS, and authentication owners; starting an already configured tunnel can expose its origin immediately.

The pinned image retains UID/GID 65532. Enrollment uses documented TUNNEL_CRED_CONTENTS from an owner-only env file, not a private bind or unsupported UID override. Credential bytes are visible to Docker operators/container processes; the account read token is never mounted or injected. No root fallback, chmod broadening or ownership repair.

A locally managed branch must bind an existing credential JSON and fresh provider account/tunnel identity with config_src=local to one owner-selected frontend/hostname, disable WARP routing, retain a final http_status:404 rule, inspect provider route inventories, and separately approve DNS/TLS/auth ownership before startup. Creating tunnels, DNS records or Access policies is outside this branch.

apps.name: Coolify
pitfalls: Installing a second deployment platform can duplicate proxy and port ownership.

A running dashboard is not proof that the first administrator, local server SSH connection, or API access is configured. The official installer can pre-create the root user with ROOT_USERNAME, ROOT_USER_EMAIL, and ROOT_USER_PASSWORD; API tokens are created after sign-in and are not an install-time bootstrap secret.
Coolify instance backups exclude deployed application data and require the separately saved APP_KEY for secret recovery.

Pinned root-user seeding validates a DNS-resolvable owner email and a mixed-case, numeric, symbol-bearing password, then disables registration. It skips an existing root rather than resetting it. Generic generated bytes or a synthetic .test email do not establish that bootstrap succeeded.
security: Coolify controls connected Docker hosts over SSH. Its official production Compose does not mount the host Docker socket; host SSH access and Docker-resource authority still require explicit approval and isolation beyond the generic scoped Compose recipe.
Keep the dashboard private during first-admin registration. Public DNS, TLS, ports 80/443, and proxy ownership require a separate ingress approval.
Protect the instance database, APP_KEY, SSH private keys, API tokens, and off-host backups as privileged recovery material.

apps.name: Dash.
pitfalls: The shared profile intentionally provides only kernel-visible CPU/RAM. Native Linux Docker normally exposes kernel-wide /proc counters; Docker VM or virtualized /proc can expose another scope. CPU and memory limits bound Dashdot, not the reported counters. Independently compare scope before claiming physical-host metrics.

Widget selection alone is insufficient: pinned LazyObservable starts every collector when background collection is enabled. The recipe disables background collection and Docker-specific namespace setup explicitly.

The adapter validates configured scope and nonempty complete CPU/RAM data, not host identity, freshness, disks/network, Homarr widgets or restart persistence. Full host observation still needs separate source-bound authority and acceptance; no privilege bypass is published.
security: The shared CPU/RAM profile grants no capabilities, namespace access or host mounts and uses a read-only root filesystem. The upstream full-host Compose grants privileged mode and host-root visibility; do not infer those grants from ordinary app approval.
Keep the unauthenticated dashboard on a private interface and review whether host inventory is appropriate for its viewers.

apps.name: Deluge
pitfalls: Daemon, Web UI, peer ports, and plugin behavior must be planned separately.
The image documents no first-start password environment variable, and post-start RPC rotation leaves a default-password window on a shared Compose network.
security: Keep the Web UI and daemon control port private and protect their authentication.
The documented initial WebUI password is shared; change and verify it before granting access or joining untrusted services to its network.
Do not advertise VPN-safe downloader egress without a recorded tunnel-break fail-closed test.

apps.name: Dockge
pitfalls: The official Compose mount gives Dockge host Docker control; importing or creating stacks needs explicit ownership and upgrade boundaries.
The stacks directory must be an absolute bind with identical host and container paths.

Pinned 1.5.0 setup and login use internal Socket.IO events, not a stable HTTP first-admin or durable API-key contract. A running UI without approved daemon authority does not satisfy Compose-management acceptance.
security: Protect the UI and treat Docker access as host control; do not mount the host Docker socket through a generic app recipe.

apps.name: Docmost
pitfalls: APP_SECRET and DATABASE_URL have no documented _FILE form; the v2 recipe uses owner-only generated environment, which remains visible to Docker inspection access. Shared first-owner setup uses the fixed admin@example.test email in this batch.
Bases and Kanban are commercial features, not included in the Community edition.
Back up PostgreSQL and local attachment storage consistently.
security: Keep the app, database, Redis, and workspace private; persist a random application secret and database credentials outside catalog or rendered manifests.

apps.name: Emby
pitfalls: License and hardware-transcoding features must be checked before selection.

First-owner setup remains manual: complete the wizard with username admin and this project's generated password before headless setup. The official authenticated System/Configuration DTO exposes IsStartupWizardCompleted, but public system info does not. No safe unauthenticated untouched-state gate is established, so the adapter never reads or writes Startup/User or Startup/Complete. After exact admin-policy and completion readback, it creates and privately saves one project-labeled Auth/Keys token, never the login session token. Incomplete/duplicate/inactive inventories and ambiguous missing keys stop without replay. Fresh-image, media playback, restart persistence, and Homarr integration remain untested.
security: Keep administration private and review remote access.

apps.name: Firefly III
pitfalls: A recoverable installation needs the database, uploads, and configuration backed up together; changing database credentials after initialization can break access.

The shared setup adapter uses the pinned web-session registration and personal-token routes; a lost one-time token response requires inspection, and the example admin@example.test login is not a usable recovery inbox. Compose start is not completed onboarding.
security: Protect finance records, application secrets, database credentials, and any importer credentials.
Keep registration and the personal-access-token creation flow private; the first registered user becomes the owner.

apps.name: Forgejo
pitfalls: Backing up repositories without database and configuration can lose metadata.

The pinned CLI privately generates the first administrator password. Setup separately creates and privately saves one read:user API token, verifies its owner, ID and exact scopes, and migrates owned administrator-only checkpoints. Missing one-time password/token output forbids replay. This read-only user token does not grant repository access or prove Git operation; Homarr integration remains unsupported. Token inventories beyond the bounded first page require inspection.
security: Protect SSH/HTTP ingress, signing keys, webhooks, and repository backups.

apps.name: FreshRSS
pitfalls: Aggressive polling can trigger source rate limits or bans.

The shared adapter never submits passwords in argv or URLs. Its exported API credential is the independent durable API password, not the Google Reader Auth value used only for verification. Foreign API passwords, lost private credentials, and incomplete uncertain writes block automatic replay. Browser form-login, feed operations, restart persistence and native Homarr integration remain unverified.
security: Protect form-login credentials; enable the separate mobile API and its distinct API password only after explicit approval.

apps.name: Frigate
pitfalls: Retention and inference load can exhaust storage or compute.

The bootstrap explicitly disables TLS only on the private authenticated 8971 listener; authentication remains enabled. Internal unauthenticated 5000 is unpublished and bound to container loopback, so the no-secret Homarr integration does not yet have an authorized service-network endpoint.

The read-only, camera-free bootstrap config pins schema version 0.18-0. Camera additions need a separately approved writable owner-configuration boundary; the starter does not provide recording, detection, camera or hardware acceptance.

Only an exact-current-start fresh-user log block may supply the temporary password; reset blocks and ambiguous logs must be refused. Rotation checkpoints before PUT and never repeats an uncertain update. A login JWT is not a durable API key.
security: Keep camera credentials secret; keep unauthenticated port 5000 unpublished; approve GPU/TPU devices explicitly.

Capture the generated admin password only from this exact owned container's current startup into an owner-only file, rotate it with an approved checkpoint, and verify authenticated access. Do not dump container logs into reports.

apps.name: Gatus
pitfalls: The starter configuration checks only Gatus itself; readiness is not evidence of monitoring other services.
Default in-memory history does not survive restart; the recipe selects SQLite on a project-owned volume.
No administrator account or API key is generated by this recipe.
security: Keep the unauthenticated dashboard and status API on loopback or a separately approved private route.
Review target URLs and alert credentials before adding real monitors; neither is in the starter recipe.

apps.name: Glances
pitfalls: The safe shared recipe monitors its own container only; host observation needs a separately approved privilege expansion.
The documented password-file bootstrap is interactive and cannot be represented by the current shared secret inputs.
security: Keep the Web UI and API private; unauthenticated API responses may expose process command lines.
Treat host PID visibility and the Docker socket as separate explicit privilege decisions.

apps.name: Gluetun
pitfalls: Gluetun's image healthcheck and firewall kill switch do not independently prove fail-closed downloader egress; verify the shared namespace and deliberate tunnel-break behavior.

The derived shared recipe consumes only the source-bound tun-net-admin runtime-resource profile, requiring its exact privilege approval and inspected local character device. It does not attach a downloader namespace or grant generic capabilities/devices.

The pinned release defaults several control routes, including VPN status writes, to unauthenticated access when no roles are configured. Existing privateConfigs prepares an explicit read-only generated-key TOML role at /run/secrets/control-auth and HTTP_CONTROL_SERVER_AUTH_CONFIG_FILEPATH selects it, replacing the permissive defaults.

The checked v3.41.3 release source retains permissive public control roles despite the current wiki describing private-by-default routes. Pin and verify the actual image behavior; do not infer authentication policy from the moving wiki.

The checked v3.40.0 and v3.41.3 VPN validators accept only OpenVPN or WireGuard with a supported provider. No documented VPN-disabled control-only mode was established; disabling the firewall or running only genkey/healthcheck is not a useful downloader VPN deployment.

Provider secret files use documented *_SECRETFILE variables, including OPENVPN_USER_SECRETFILE, OPENVPN_PASSWORD_SECRETFILE, and WIREGUARD_CONF_SECRETFILE. The owner must select provider and protocol; generated control credentials are not VPN provider credentials.

Control bootstrap acceptance must reject an unauthenticated status request, authenticate the saved read-only credential, and read VPN status. This proves control access only; downloader wiring and tunnel-break privacy acceptance remain separate.

The app-local derived-recipe.ts and discovered setup.ts consume control.ts directly. Setup readiness means only anonymous denial, saved read-only key acceptance and running VPN status; it does not claim write-policy tests, downloader IP/DNS privacy, tunnel-break or restart evidence.

Only explicit protonvpn or purevpn provider selections with openvpn and one server-country are supported by this shared profile. Import the provider's issued OpenVPN username and password as separate mode-0600 files; ProtonVPN web-account credentials are not its OpenVPN credentials. Other providers and WireGuard remain separate reviewed profiles.
Provider and protocol requirements differ; do not embed OPENVPN_USER, OPENVPN_PASSWORD, WIREGUARD_PRIVATE_KEY, or equivalent secret payloads in catalog environment fields.
security: Select a supported VPN provider and OpenVPN or WireGuard protocol before apply; provider-specific credentials and WireGuard private keys stay at the private apply boundary.
Approve NET_ADMIN and /dev/net/tun explicitly; keep Gluetun's firewall enabled, attach only the downloader to its network namespace, and publish the downloader WebUI only on a private gateway bind.
Require a recorded tunnel-break test showing downloader external IP and DNS requests fail while the downloader remains running, followed by tunnel restoration.

Homarr's native Gluetun integration is separate from gateway acceptance. Use an explicit read-only control role and saved private API key; do not select the integration's unauthenticated alternative or expose VPN control writes.

apps.name: Gotify
pitfalls: The default username and password initialize only when Gotify first creates its database; an existing /app/data volume keeps its current account and must be inspected if login fails.
Gotify 3.x returns application tokens only on creation or rotation; if the one-time create response is lost, stop for inspection instead of retrying.
Delivery outside the private network needs TLS and a deliberate mobile connectivity path.
security: Protect application tokens, user accounts, message contents, and WebSocket ingress.

apps.name: Grafana
pitfalls: Dashboards without a durable data source do not provide monitoring history.
The image runs as UID 472, which cannot read host-owner mode-0600 secret mounts. The reviewed private env-file bootstrap keeps the image user unchanged; Docker operators can inspect its environment.
security: Protect administration and data-source credentials.

apps.name: HAProxy
pitfalls: The official image has no default configuration and runs as haproxy UID/GID 99. Only the publisher-evidenced non-secret configuration may be container-readable; generated passwords and hash env files remain owner-private. Do not change the container to root or relax private files.
Configuration reload and certificate lifecycle need explicit ownership.
security: Protect statistics/admin endpoints and certificate material.
Keep the listener private until a separately approved ingress route has one DNS/TLS/auth owner.

apps.name: Headscale
pitfalls: The hosted container guide is community-maintained and explicitly not developer-verified. Its read-only root, writable /var/run/headscale tmpfs, read-only /etc/headscale config mount, and persistent /var/lib/headscale need pinned-source and image verification. The version-matched config defaults server_url and listen_addr to 127.0.0.1, which cannot serve real clients unchanged; container listen_addr must bind an interface reachable from the published port.

First identity setup is headscale users create <USER>; headscale users list resolves its ID; headscale preauthkeys create --user <USER_ID> issues a default one-hour, single-use registration key. A safe setup adapter would need bounded local CLI execution, private capture of the one-time key, and replay-safe inspection without putting it in argv, logs, or ordinary reports.
Control-plane failure can block enrollment and make recovery circular.
A loopback /health response cannot prove the configured server URL, DNS/TLS route, node registration, or mesh traffic. Require a real client enrollment and peer connectivity check before acceptance.

headscale apikeys create prints the API key only once and defaults to a 90-day expiry; list returns prefixes and metadata, not the credential. Reuse checkpointed container.exec and private secrets.writeApiKey rather than an app-specific command router; their crash window still needs a capture/reconciliation contract distinct from admin-password capture. A lost create response cannot be recovered by listing keys or justify automatic re-creation.

The derived recipe binds the reviewed canonical HTTPS identity into server_url. API-key setup uses the saved private loopback origin; it does not install ingress, establish client DNS/TLS trust, or prove the required control-protocol proxy behavior. Those remain separate approvals and acceptance gates.
security: Protect one-time API and node-registration keys, local CLI/socket administration, and the SQLite/private-key state. A Headscale user is a node identity, not a password-based administrator account; a preauthkey enrolls a node and is not an API key.

Assign one approved DNS/TLS/443 owner before making the control plane reachable to clients. A reverse proxy must support Headscale's POST WebSocket upgrade with the tailscale-control-protocol header; Cloudflare Proxy and Tunnel do not. Keep metrics and gRPC administration private.

apps.name: Homarr
pitfalls: A generic link is not evidence that a dedicated integration or widget works.
security: Keep integration credentials in Homarr encrypted storage and protect API keys.

apps.name: Home Assistant
pitfalls: Container mode does not provide the same add-on lifecycle as Home Assistant OS.
Loopback-only bridge networking does not provide the LAN discovery behavior of the upstream host-network example.
A smart-speaker experience also needs compatible audio hardware plus chosen wake-word, speech-to-text, and text-to-speech components; Home Assistant alone is not a physical speaker.

Shared setup verifies the owner and integration token, but reports unfinished core_config, analytics and integration wizard steps separately. Core-config completion starts upstream provider flows; it is not silently approved by account creation or Homarr publication.
security: The bounded Compose recipe exposes only the web UI on loopback; approve LAN access, host networking, USB radios, microphones, speakers, and public exposure separately.

apps.name: Homebridge
pitfalls: The official Docker Compose requires network_mode: host for HomeKit discovery and persists /homebridge. The private administration recipe deliberately omits host networking; successful login is not LAN discovery or pairing acceptance.

The pinned first-admin adapter checkpoints before creation and never replays an ambiguous write. Its authenticated API credential is an expiring Bearer session, not a durable API key; tokens are not exported as keys.
Fresh-instance setup, lost-response replay and restart persistence have not been verified against a live image.
Third-party plugins have independent maintenance and privilege profiles.
security: This recipe publishes administration on loopback and disables Avahi. Host networking for actual HomeKit discovery needs separate LAN exposure and port ownership approval.
UI 5.29.0 creates its first administrator through a guarded setup wizard. Saved-password login and administrator readback must succeed before permitting LAN access or installing plugins.

apps.name: Immich
pitfalls: PostgreSQL belongs on suitable local storage; back up database and originals.
security: Keep originals private and protect mobile/session credentials.

apps.name: Jellyfin
pitfalls: Hardware acceleration depends on matching host drivers and devices.
security: Keep administration private and approve any GPU device access.

apps.name: Keycloak
pitfalls: Development-mode quick starts are not production templates.
A loopback-only HTTP container is not a complete TLS-backed identity-provider deployment.
security: Use production mode with a production database, TLS, an explicit hostname, protected admin access, and realm export/recovery.

apps.name: Kopia
pitfalls: The generated repository password does not create or connect a repository; keep it available for an owner-approved repository setup.
Kopia does not issue an API key during this server-password bootstrap. The saved admin password only verifies private UI access, not backup readiness.
The current Compose recipe has no repository or snapshot-source mount. A local filesystem repository would live on the same host and would not satisfy the off-host-repository dependency by itself.
Repository availability, snapshot sources, and isolated restore must be tested independently.
security: Protect repository password, server credentials, and retention policy.

apps.name: Lidarr
pitfalls: Path mismatches and music metadata availability can prevent reliable imports.

The pinned Lidarr API uses /api/v1, unlike the Sonarr/Radarr /api/v3 route. The candidate shared adapter configures Forms login only; music root, downloader wiring, and restart persistence still need direct acceptance.
security: Treat API keys as secrets and keep management access private.

apps.name: Linkwarden
pitfalls: Captured content can create storage growth and legal retention questions.

Shared setup checkpoints first-owner login and a saved API token before an exact reviewed Compose environment transition. Rerun shared setup after transition for saved-login, token, and anonymous registration-denial readback; a failed denial probe may create an extra account and requires inspection. Archive roundtrip and restart persistence remain separate acceptance checks.
security: Keep the service private, use distinct random NEXTAUTH_SECRET, POSTGRES_PASSWORD, and MEILI_MASTER_KEY values, and protect archived content and access tokens.

apps.name: LLDAP
pitfalls: LDAP support does not imply OIDC or forward-auth support.
security: Protect directory credentials, administration, and backup exports.

apps.name: Loki
pitfalls: High-cardinality labels and unrestricted retention increase cost and risk.
security: Redact secrets and personal data before log ingestion.

apps.name: Mayan EDMS
pitfalls: Workflow complexity is substantially higher than a PDF toolbox.

The upstream defaults contain database, broker, and Redis passwords. The shared candidate generates private credentials and derives the required configuration without exposing passwords in command arguments.

The pinned autoadmin implementation displays even a supplied initial password on the login page. Keep bootstrap private; setup authenticates the saved owner before rehashing that same password to clear the display, then verifies it is gone. Never reset an unknown owner or repeat an ambiguous token request.

The image starts as root for its documented initialization, then runs application processes as mayan. Redis uses the current host UID to read the owner-only generated configuration; verify this identity and file readability on the intended Docker context before live acceptance.
security: Define document permissions and recovery before ingestion.

apps.name: MinIO AIStor (licensed)
pitfalls: S3 compatibility does not make one-node storage highly available or a backup.
The community repository is archived and source-only; do not infer a maintained image from historical Docker examples.
AIStor uses separate S3 API (9000) and console (9001) ports. A private API listener alone does not provide console access or secure either endpoint.

AIStor requires an operator-obtained license file supplied through --license or the documented MINIO_LICENSE file-path variable. It is not an application-generated API key. The explicit derived recipe imports this file independently of root onboarding and uses MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD_FILE for the generated secret. Neither file preparation nor S3 root authentication proves a valid license. Do not invent MINIO_LICENSE_FILE or use file: URI syntax.

Additional private port descriptors already represent S3 9000 and console 9001, but setup HTTP still uses one saved origin. Authenticate the S3 API with a canonical signed request; console HTTP 200, unauthenticated health, and root credentials are not a newly provisioned scoped durable API key.
AIStor Free does not provide distributed high availability or server-side encryption at rest.
security: Set unique, long, random root credentials before startup; AIStor otherwise defaults both values to minioadmin. Protect bucket policies, TLS, and administrative access; expose the S3 API and console only on approved private paths.

apps.name: Navidrome
pitfalls: Library scanning and metadata behavior depend on stable paths, tags, and file ownership.
The native UI authentication routes are version-pinned implementation details, not a stable public API; re-verify before upgrading.
security: Protect user accounts, listening data, media paths, and any public streaming route.

apps.name: NetBird
pitfalls: Self-hosting the control plane adds availability and recovery dependencies.

The first-owner setup endpoint is unauthenticated until setup completes; inspect GET /api/instance first. NB_SETUP_PAT_ENABLED=true and create_pat=true permit POST /api/setup to return a one-time PAT, followed by GET /api/users with Authorization: Token. Keep the response private and never replay setup after an ambiguous response; the PAT defaults to one day and needs a reviewed expiry/rotation policy.

The pinned installer offers use-ip over HTTP, but that is an explicit different identity/exposure choice, not permission to substitute a loopback HTTP URL for reviewed HTTPS. External-proxy mode keeps HTTP frontends private but still exposes STUN separately and requires path-specific HTTP/WebSocket and h2c/gRPC routing.

The selectable shared derived recipe binds the explicit canonical origin and exact private proxy address into privateConfigs with standard padded Base64 session/store keys. The protocol-aware HTTPS route is a separate reviewed boundary and does not authorize public exposure or establish peer connectivity.
A healthy dashboard or server does not prove peer enrollment, remote connectivity, or route access.

The app-owned setup adapter implements pinned setup JSON, fresh-instance checks, attempted-write replay refusal and private PAT capture followed by authenticated owner/PAT metadata readback. Fresh local password login uses a private retained PKCE attempt, one-use code and temporary Bearer readback. Expired or lost PAT requires explicit reconciliation, never an automatic replacement; external SSO and native peer connectivity are not configured or proven.
security: Protect owner credentials, setup-time tokens, generated server secrets, and persistent control-plane state.
Approve a public DNS/TLS/80/443 owner and UDP 3478 reachability separately; do not infer a LAN or subnet route from a running control plane.

apps.name: Netdata
pitfalls: The bounded candidate cannot provide host, sibling-container, Docker, systemd, or network-namespace monitoring.
The official full-host example requires host PID and network namespaces, SYS_PTRACE and SYS_ADMIN, broad read-only host mounts, and a Docker socket mount; it is not represented by this recipe.
security: The bundled candidate uses loopback HTTP, no host mounts or added capabilities, and no Cloud claim. Review any host-observation expansion separately.

apps.name: Nextcloud
pitfalls: Cloud collaboration is heavier than device-to-device folder sync.
security: Require TLS, protected administration, and coordinated database/data backup.

apps.name: Nginx Proxy Manager
pitfalls: GUI state can diverge from generated project configuration.
The login API issues bearer tokens, not a documented durable API key.

Do not supply INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD to this pinned image: backend/setup.js logs it at INFO during fresh-database bootstrap. The first-user HTTP adapter checks setup mode, checkpoints before creation, and verifies the saved email/password without replaying an uncertain creation.
security: Keep the admin interface private and protect certificate data.
Public 80/443, DNS and TLS ownership require a separate ingress approval.

apps.name: Node-RED
pitfalls: The default settings file does not enable editor or Admin API authentication; private port binding alone is not administrator setup.
POST /auth/token returns an expiring access token; do not hand it off as a durable API key.
A flow editor can become a broad control plane without clear ownership.
security: Configure adminAuth with a bcrypt-hashed password in /data/settings.js before exposing the editor or Admin API.
Review contributed nodes and every credential or host integration used by flows.

apps.name: ntfy
pitfalls: Guessable or anonymous topics can leak operational alerts when default access is not deny-all.

The shared recipe seeds an administrator and creates one non-expiring Homarr token with administrator privileges; separate least-privilege publisher credentials, topic ACLs, and notification delivery are not automated.
An administrator token grants broad account privileges; ntfy access tokens are not individually scoped to topics.
security: Set auth-file and auth-default-access=deny-all; the documented default is read-write even when authentication is enabled.
Provision an administrator and separate least-privilege publisher account before enabling notification delivery or public exposure.

apps.name: NZBGet
pitfalls: The archived legacy repository and images can be mistaken for the maintained successor.
The official Docker image documents NZBGET_PASS as a plain environment variable, not a file-backed secret; shared Compose must generate its private environment file before the container starts.
NZBGet RPC uses username/password pairs and does not document an API key.
security: Keep provider credentials and the control interface on a private network; the RPC control interface uses HTTP Basic authentication unless HTTPS is configured.
Change the documented default control password before exposing the interface to another device.

apps.name: Ollama
pitfalls: Model downloads are large and each model has its own license and memory needs.
security: Bind the model API privately and approve GPU device access.

apps.name: Open WebUI
pitfalls: A chat UI can expose a privately bound model API if ingress is misconfigured.
Headless admin creation applies only to an empty user database; later restarts do not reset an existing password.
API keys require an enabled global setting, are user-scoped, and creating another key replaces the old one.
security: Keep the first-start admin password and persistent WEBUI_SECRET_KEY private; protect accounts, conversation history, provider keys, and tool integrations.

apps.name: Pangolin
pitfalls: The full server is not a drop-in answer for a CGNAT-only home host.
The official installer generates a multi-container public ingress stack and asks for deployment-specific domains and Let's Encrypt email; a loopback-bound shared recipe would not reproduce it.
Container start does not complete token-based first-admin registration or organization creation.

The documented no-tunneling mode removes Gerbil and its extra capabilities, but still requires selected dashboard/base domains, HTTPS origin, certificate owner, private server secret, and separately approved Traefik routes. It is not evidence that outbound tunnels work.

The documented pangctl set-admin-credentials command takes plaintext --password in argv. Do not use it for generated private credentials; a pinned-source HTTP bootstrap with privately captured setup token and replay-safe owner checks is still needed.

The shared recipe consumes non-secret generated config with SERVER_SECRET_FILE and a distinct generated PANGOLIN_SETUP_TOKEN capability; neither is an administrator password. Existing administrators are not adopted automatically.

The private administrative proxy installs dashboard/API routing only. It does not install the dynamic resource provider, Badger authentication plugin, public DNS/TLS, Gerbil, WireGuard, organizations or resources.

Ready means the exact first administrator and saved root-key metadata were read back. It does not prove Integration API authentication/action grants, organization or resource access, intended-client trust or restart persistence.
security: Require separate approval for a public VPS, domain and TLS ownership, and firewall exposure of TCP 80/443 and UDP 51820/21820 before server deployment.
Keep the initial-setup token from container logs and connector credentials out of plans, reports, and screenshots; verify the first admin and organization separately.
Gerbil's NET_ADMIN/SYS_MODULE capabilities and Traefik's shared Gerbil network namespace require a separately reviewed privilege boundary; ordinary app setup must not grant them.

apps.name: Paperless-ngx
pitfalls: Network filesystems may require polling; database and archive restore together.
security: Treat document contents as sensitive and control ingest paths.

apps.name: Passbolt
pitfalls: The derived shared recipe binds explicit SMTP relay, sender, server-key and HTTPS identity choices before start and generates private database passwords. It supports only an owner-approved no-auth STARTTLS relay. Native first-admin enrollment/login is source-implemented; time synchronization, SMTP delivery, client import, encrypted-vault acceptance and recovery remain independently unverified.
Working SMTP and time sync are installation prerequisites; test delivery of a real registration/recovery email independently of container or HTTP health.

First-admin creation uses the official register_user command with an owner-selected email, first name, last name, and admin role. It returns a one-time setup URL, not a password; the current headless HTTP onboarding patterns cannot safely claim completion of the browser extension, owner passphrase, and recovery-kit flow.
Preserve the database, server GPG keys, configuration, and the official Compose JWT volume across recreation. A database-only backup or container restart is not a recovery drill.
Changing the full base URL after users enroll can unlink browser extensions.

Native setup captures the pinned www-data register_user invitation privately, saves encrypted client-key/passphrase/recovery custody before activation, and verifies the exact administrator via server-key-verified GPGAuth. It never creates a fake local password or API key; SMTP delivery, official-client key import and encrypted-vault acceptance remain separate.

Official CE tag 5.16.0-1-ce was verified through publisher metadata on 2026-10-03: index sha256:dc7298c2847e406154beea5c4c82062828e0b1690d1d9869b2dbeae6f6e70bfc with Linux amd64, arm64 and arm images. Re-resolve and bind the selected platform digest before apply; this metadata proves neither a running server nor encrypted-client acceptance.

Private self-signed HTTPS is documented; public DNS and ACME are not mandatory. Stable private name resolution and intended-client certificate trust still need evidence. A generated application password cannot substitute for the owner's GPG key/passphrase and recovery custody.

The documented Go CLI requires an already-enrolled private key and passphrase; configure is not enrollment. The upstream Go library's SetupAccount returns the generated private key only after setup completion, so a direct wrapper risks key loss after activation. A reviewed client runtime must persist approved key/recovery custody before setup completion and reconcile the saved user/key after ambiguous outcomes.
security: Require an owner-chosen, stable private HTTPS origin with trusted TLS and matching APP_FULL_BASE_URL before registration or client use; do not substitute a loopback HTTP URL or publish 80/443 without separate edge approval.

Keep database and SMTP credentials, server GPG and JWT keys, first-registration link, recovery kit, and administrative access private; back up the database, GPG keys, and configuration together and prove an isolated restore.

apps.name: PatchMon
pitfalls: Inventory freshness is not proof that patches installed successfully or that reboots completed.

Redis authentication must remain enabled. Its generated private configuration keeps the password out of command arguments; no Redis healthcheck is claimed because upstream's documented check exposes the password in argv. The server's pinned startup authenticates and pings Redis before serving HTTP; an initial failure exits and relies on its restart policy.

CORS_ORIGIN derives from the selected loopback origin. A different browser-facing private URL requires separately reviewed origin configuration; a running container is not CORS or dashboard acceptance.

The pinned headless adapter uses setup-admin, saved-password login, and superadmin profile readback with checkpointed first-owner creation. It requires an owner-selected email and a password satisfying the effective upstream policy; fresh-image and restart acceptance have not been run.

Login JWTs are short-lived session credentials, not durable integration API keys. Default dashboard setup creates no Homarr token. The optional once-returned key/secret pair is saved atomically in a private JSON file, inventory/readback verified and tested against the GetHomepage stats API; lost unsaved secrets require manual reconciliation, not token replay. No setup branch installs root/sudo agents, enrolls hosts, enables remote access or runs patches.
security: Protect agent enrollment and inventory because they reveal host and package details.
Keep the server private; protect database, Redis, JWT, session, and AI encryption secrets.

The v2.1.3 host enrollment handler accepts active token pairs without checking integration_type. Even Homarr/GetHomepage statistics credentials can enroll hosts; create them only after explicit credential-authority=stats-and-enrollment choice and exact token approval. The adapter limits them to one host per day and never enrolls a host.

apps.name: PeaNUT
pitfalls: PeaNUT does not provision a NUT server, UPS driver, device, or connection credentials; those require an owner-selected existing installation.
WEB_USERNAME and WEB_PASSWORD create the initial account only; changing them later does not rotate the stored password.
v6.0.0 defaults auth.yaml outside /config; the shared recipe relies on environment bootstrap only and cannot claim auth-file persistence until the path defect is resolved.
A green dashboard does not prove load runtime, shutdown sequencing, or recovery after power returns.
security: Keep PeaNUT authenticated and privately reachable; its API exposes UPS commands as well as monitoring.
Keep NUT control credentials private and separate read-only monitoring from shutdown authority.

apps.name: PhotoPrism
pitfalls: Indexing cost and database choice depend on library size.

Public mode can return a successful session without validating the password. Setup requires anonymous session denial, exact active admin identity and role, and authenticated session readback; a session ID alone is not administrator proof.

Setup saves one genuine user-bound API app password with read-only scope and a one-year lifetime. Disabled app passwords, expired credentials, lost creation output, or identity/scope/lifetime mismatch require inspection; setup never rotates or repeats an uncertain creation. Photo ingestion and restart persistence remain separate acceptance checks.
security: Keep originals private and publish only through approved ingress.

apps.name: Pi-hole
pitfalls: The private admin recipe does not publish DNS port 53 or provide LAN DNS service.
Port 53 and system resolver conflicts can disrupt the entire LAN.
security: Keep administration private and confirm DNS/DHCP ownership before publishing network ports.

apps.name: Plex
pitfalls: Features and account requirements vary by subscription and release.
The image ignores PLEX_CLAIM after the server is already logged in, so retries must inspect existing ownership before changing claim state.

The upstream bootstrap writes /.firstRunComplete even when claim exchange fails. An expired or invalid first-run claim requires explicit inspection and reviewed recovery; restarting or rerunning extraction does not automatically retry claiming.

The unauthenticated /identity endpoint reports claimed status and machine identity, not the owning Plex account; a local HTTP 200 or claimed=true is insufficient acceptance. The owner must verify the server in their Plex account before any claim of first-run completion.
security: Treat the Plex claim token and resulting server token as private account credentials.
Keep the server port private until claim ownership is verified; remote access and discovery ports need separate review.

Do not put PLEX_CLAIM in catalog data, a generated Compose file, or Docker command arguments. Use the upstream bootstrap's PLEX_CLAIM_FILE with an owner-issued private token; a generated password cannot replace the account-bound claim token.
Never enable DEBUG: the upstream bootstrap's shell tracing can expose claim and server tokens.

apps.name: Portainer
pitfalls: A management UI can mutate projects it does not own.

The disconnected recipe uses manual-first-admin only for generated admin identity metadata; --admin-password-file performs first-account seeding, not POST /api/users/admin/init. No socket, agent or remote Docker endpoint is supplied.
A Portainer server without a connected, authenticated Docker environment and owner-authorized readback is not accepted as a working container manager.

Fresh Portainer CE 2.39.4+ instances require a setup token unless an administrator password is pre-seeded with --admin-password-file; POST /api/users/admin/init alone neither bypasses that gate nor proves endpoint ownership. Do not copy the log-issued setup token or administrator password into commands or ordinary reports.

Portainer API keys inherit their user's permissions. Pinned 2.45.1 supports POST /api/users/{id}/tokens using that user's authenticated session and password, returning rawAPIKey once; GET inventory cannot recover it. Checkpoint before creation, save before follow-up verification, and never replay an unsaved ambiguous create.
security: Treat socket, Agent, and remote Docker API access as host-wide Docker authority. Require explicit privilege approval and a separately reviewed access boundary; never mount the host socket through the generic recipe or expose an unauthenticated Docker API. For a remote API, require mutually authenticated TLS with certificate verification.

apps.name: PostgreSQL
pitfalls: Volume copies of a live database are not automatically consistent backups.
pg_isready reports server availability, not password authentication or application readiness.
security: Default published port binds only to loopback. Do not expose PostgreSQL publicly; keep generated credentials in private files.

apps.name: Prometheus
pitfalls: Unbounded cardinality and retention can consume storage rapidly.
security: Keep scrape targets and management endpoints private.

apps.name: Prowlarr
pitfalls: Indexer availability and acceptable use are external constraints.
security: Protect indexer credentials and API keys as secrets.

apps.name: qBittorrent
pitfalls: The WebUI and peer-listener ports are separate; do not publish peer ports without an explicit choice.
VPN status alone does not prove a working kill switch.
security: Keep the WebUI private and separately approve downloader VPN routing.
Verify the selected image's first-run credential mechanism before automating login; do not assume another publisher's temporary-password log format.

apps.name: Radarr
pitfalls: Mismatched downloader and library paths break imports and hardlinks.
security: Treat API keys as secrets and keep the management UI private.

apps.name: Renovate
pitfalls: The open-source image needs an external cron-like scheduler; a continuously running Compose service is not the documented execution model.
Repository selection and token permissions require an explicit operator choice before scheduling any update job.
RENOVATE_TOKEN is documented, but a generic RENOVATE_TOKEN_FILE input is not established here; do not fabricate a file variable or put a Personal Access Token in process arguments.
An image update PR does not prove migration or restore compatibility.
security: A Forgejo deployment requires a dedicated Renovate account and user-created Personal Access Token with the documented repository permissions; setup cannot safely generate or infer that token.
Scope repository and registry tokens to the minimum required access, and pass them only at the job's secret boundary.

apps.name: restic
pitfalls: Restic does not schedule backups; a recurring job needs an external scheduler and overlap protection.
A CLI container has no administrator or frontend port; the manual profile is inert on ordinary apply and its version probe does not prove backup coverage.
The recipe's managed source and repository folders are empty staging placeholders, not selected production data or an independent off-host copy.
A successful snapshot or repository check is not proof that application state restores; perform an isolated restore.
security: Keep the repository password and backend credentials in private secret storage; retain the password independently for recovery.
Choose and verify an off-host repository target before claiming backup coverage.

apps.name: SABnzbd
pitfalls: Provider access and retention are external operational dependencies.
Select completed and incomplete paths with the Arr import layout; differing paths or filesystems can prevent hardlinks or atomic moves.
security: Treat provider credentials, server configuration, and the SABnzbd API key as secrets.
Keep its WebUI private; the API key is accepted as a query parameter by the upstream API.

apps.name: Scrypted
pitfalls: The shared recipe is a minimal bridge-only administrator bootstrap, not an equivalent full camera deployment. The upstream Compose comments describe bridge networking; HomeKit requires separately approved mDNS/Avahi integration, and camera reachability must be verified directly.
The upstream example includes a Watchtower service with Docker socket access and unpinned default images; it is not a safe drop-in project recipe.

Pinned source implements first administrator creation through POST /login and durable user-token readback through authenticated GET /login. The latter can consume a reset-login marker and erase users; the adapter checks its absence and treats the request as an approved effect. Do not create that marker concurrently.

Login and durable-token identity are read back, but the first owner's administrator role is inferred from pinned creation source, not independently verified through an ACL-only endpoint. Camera streams, HomeKit discovery, GPU acceleration, licensed NVR recording, backup restore and restart persistence remain separate. Fresh-image and replay acceptance are unverified.
security: The bootstrap publishes only the insecure HTTP management listener on loopback. Do not expose it remotely without separately reviewed HTTPS ingress; protect administrator tokens and camera credentials.
Approve NVR storage, GPU or USB device passthrough, mDNS/Avahi access, and automatic update authority separately; none are implied by this catalog record.

apps.name: Seafile
pitfalls: The official image uses initial-admin, database, and JWT environment secrets; Docker operators can inspect container environment.
The shared recipe verifies administrator login only; library/file round-trip, client sync, restart persistence, and isolated restore remain separate acceptance gates.
Seafile's configured hostname and protocol must match the selected access route, including a nondefault host port.
security: Keep the private HTTP bind private; require TLS before exposing the service, and recover database and file data together.

apps.name: Seerr
pitfalls: The first-run flow needs owner-selected media-server credentials, libraries, and Sonarr/Radarr endpoints and API keys; use service DNS rather than localhost between containers.
Back up existing Overseerr/Jellyseerr data before first start because migration is automatic and forward-only.
security: Keep media-server credentials and Sonarr/Radarr API keys in secret storage; scope public access separately.

apps.name: Slskd
pitfalls: Only share or download content the operator is authorized to distribute or retain.
A loopback-only port 50300 does not make the daemon reachable to Soulseek peers; peer ingress needs a separate network approval.
The Soulseek protocol account requires operator-supplied credentials; Web UI credentials do not create that account.
security: Set a generated Web UI password and primary API key before first start; never retain the documented slskd/slskd defaults.
Keep the Web UI private. API keys sent over plain HTTP can be intercepted; use a trusted HTTPS route for remote clients.
Review shared folders and the Soulseek listen port separately from Web UI access.

apps.name: Sonarr
pitfalls: Mismatched downloader and library paths break imports and hardlinks.
security: Treat API keys as secrets and keep the management UI private.

apps.name: Speedtest Tracker
pitfalls: Frequent tests consume bandwidth and can distort application traffic or provider usage limits.

The pinned shared setup checks the seeded administrator inside the exact Laravel container and creates one scoped Sanctum token. If token creation commits but its one-time plaintext is lost before private storage, stop for explicit recovery rather than creating another token. Browser login UX and an actual measurement remain separate acceptance checks.
security: Keep the web UI private, replace the documented default admin login on first start, and treat public IP, ISP, and location metadata as private operational data.

apps.name: Stalwart Mail Server
pitfalls: Residential IP reputation, blocked outbound ports, and DNS errors can break delivery.
The first boot exposes only a temporary bootstrap administrator on HTTP port 8080; it does not start mail services until configuration is completed.

The wizard requires a server hostname and mail domain, writes config.json, and provisions a distinct permanent administrator; the bootstrap password is not the final administrator password. The pinned Bootstrap JMAP handler generates the permanent password and returns it once with the login identity; privately capture that response before another request, and do not replay bootstrap after losing the returned credential.

Default bootstrap prints its temporary password in container output. A pinned STALWART_RECOVERY_ADMIN avoids generating that temporary password but remains a recovery credential, not the permanent administrator or mail acceptance. Never print startup logs in ordinary setup evidence.

A production mail deployment needs selected SMTP and client ports, hostname and domain DNS records, working TLS, and external delivery checks; a private loopback WebUI alone is not a mail-server acceptance test.
STALWART_RECOVERY_ADMIN must be removed after permanent administrator and HTTPS access are verified; leaving it enabled retains a recovery login.

Community code is AGPL-3.0 licensed; enterprise functionality has a separate owner-issued license. Neither is the server-generated, once-returned management API key, which does not authenticate SMTP or IMAP.
security: Require anti-abuse controls, TLS, DNS authentication, and account recovery.

An ordinary app approval does not authorize public SMTP/client ports, DNS changes, or a TLS owner. Review the exact hostname, mail domain, listener ports, outbound policy and anti-abuse scope separately before production deployment.

apps.name: Stirling PDF
pitfalls: A PDF toolbox is not a durable document archive or backup.
security: Process sensitive PDFs only on a trusted private route.

apps.name: Syncthing
pitfalls: Synchronization propagates deletions and is not a backup.
An unpublished peer/discovery port or container bridge can leave the GUI running while device sync is unusable.
The documented offline credential generator and API-key-protected REST configuration need an exact private-file/container-operation primitive before shared setup can claim readiness.
security: Authenticate and restrict the GUI before any non-loopback exposure; the official Docker image listens on all container interfaces by default.
Protect the device private key and API key; review each device and folder share separately.

apps.name: Tailscale
pitfalls: A running container or local daemon status does not prove the node is registered and authorized in the intended tailnet. TS_ENABLE_HEALTH_CHECK exposes /healthz, but HTTP 200 proves only that the node has at least one tailnet IP, not intended-client access or ACL enforcement.

The portless private-connector recipe publishes no host frontend and joins only the shared owner frontend bridge plus its private network. It starts /usr/local/bin/tailscaled directly instead of containerboot, so credential import and Compose apply do not implicitly enroll or activate Serve.

The pinned containerboot rejects TS_DEST_IP and TS_EXPERIMENTAL_DEST_DNS_NAME when TS_USERSPACE is enabled. These forwarding settings cannot replace a reviewed private Serve configuration without separately approved kernel-network privileges.

The daemon writes /var/lib/tailscale/tailscaled.state into its owned persistent volume. Enrollment must use a non-ephemeral owner-issued key and a reviewed retention/revocation policy; local node status cannot prove the key's remote policy. Never copy the key payload into a Compose environment file.

Serve is private while Funnel is public; they are different approval classes. TS_SERVE_CONFIG can configure either, so any imported Serve configuration needs an explicit no-Funnel review and an exact owned upstream target. Upstream requires a directory bind, not an individual file bind, to detect configuration updates.

A reusable private-connector contract must bind the selected same-owner app/service/port, persistent node identity, owner-file enrollment and ACL owner into approval. Reject Funnel, subnet routes, exit-node settings and SSH; verify tailscale status --json and tailscale serve status --json without claiming intended-client access from local status alone.
security: Enrollment requires an owner-supplied auth-key file kept outside catalog data and command arguments. The pinned tailscale up CLI consumes --auth-key=file:/run/secrets/auth-key directly; shared import saves owner-only bytes, while the ordinary recipe starts only a daemon and performs no enrollment.

Default userspace networking does not route the host or sibling containers. Kernel networking requires separately approved /dev/net/tun and NET_ADMIN; subnet routes, exit-node use, Serve, and public Funnel each need separate review.

apps.name: Tdarr
pitfalls: A bad transcode policy can replace source media; test on copies and preserve recoverable originals.
The documented seededApiKey setting creates a key, not a first-admin identity. The headless adapter separately registers the first admin, verifies login, and saves an owned API key before insertion.
Port 8266 is the server/API listener and is not published by the shared recipe; only the web UI is mapped to loopback.
The internal node starts with zero configured workers; approve library write behavior and test on copies before enabling transcoding.
security: Limit worker access to owner-selected libraries and approve GPU or device access explicitly.
Keep the first-user setup screen private; auth=true does not pre-create an administrator or close registration.

apps.name: Technitium DNS Server
pitfalls: A broad DNS feature set increases configuration and recovery scope.
The shared recipe publishes only the loopback web console. DNS on TCP/UDP 53 requires a separate LAN owner and cutover plan.
security: Separate public authoritative service from private recursion and administration.

apps.name: Tracearr
pitfalls: Session analytics are not a replacement for service readiness or host monitoring.
The standard image requires TimescaleDB, not plain PostgreSQL, and a secret-bearing DATABASE_URL.
The current official pg18 Compose example calls PostgreSQL 18 experimental and new-install-only; never reuse an existing data volume with it.
The bundled local-owner adapter requires a reviewed email, refuses an existing uncheckpointed owner or claim-code setup, and never repeats an uncertain signup or API-key rotation.
Owner and API-key setup does not enroll a media server, fetch media, configure notifications, or prove Homarr integration or restart persistence.
security: Treat session history, user identities, IP data, and media-server API access as sensitive.

apps.name: Traefik
pitfalls: The recipe never enables insecure API/dashboard access. Control-interface credentials do not create Traefik user records; existing owners are not silently migrated or given replacement credentials.
security: Protect the Docker API and authenticate the dashboard.

apps.name: Transmission
pitfalls: This private recipe does not publish the TCP/UDP peer port or establish a VPN kill switch. Incoming peers and VPN-safe downloading require separately approved work.
security: Keep the authenticated RPC/WebUI bound to loopback; separately approve peer-port publication and downloader VPN routing.

apps.name: Umami
pitfalls: Self-hosting does not remove consent, retention, or data-governance duties.
The seeded administrator is reachable on the selected loopback origin until the separately approved password-rotation setup completes; never expose it more broadly before rotation is verified.
security: Keep administration private, change the seeded admin/umami password immediately, generate unique APP_SECRET and TWO_FACTOR_ENCRYPTION_KEY values, and minimize collected visitor data.

apps.name: Unbound
pitfalls: An open recursive resolver creates abuse and availability risk.
security: Restrict recursion to intended clients and keep controls private.

apps.name: Uptime Kuma
pitfalls: Its data path requires POSIX locks and is not supported on NFS.
security: Protect the admin UI and notification credentials.

Creating an API key globally changes /metrics authentication from administrator Basic auth to API-key Basic auth. These keys do not authenticate the status-page API or the administrator's Socket.IO API. Setup creates and rotates no keys.

apps.name: Valkey
pitfalls: Do not assume Redis and Valkey versions are interchangeable for every application.
The official image has no documented generated-password-file bootstrap; unauthenticated PING or container liveness does not prove safe peer access or a secure deployment.
security: Keep TCP port 6379 loopback-only on the host and restrict the shared Compose network to trusted applications. The no-account recipe has no authentication; require separately reviewed ACL or requirepass configuration before any untrusted peer or broader exposure.

apps.name: Vaultwarden
pitfalls: Compatibility and recovery are higher consequence than an ordinary web app.
The built-in admin page is disabled without ADMIN_TOKEN; enabling it is separate from creating a vault owner and must not substitute for HTTPS or signup controls.

SIGNUPS_ALLOWED=false closes ordinary registration, but organization invitations and admin invitations have separate behavior. A nonempty SIGNUPS_DOMAINS_WHITELIST and persisted config.json overrides must also be checked before claiming registration closure.

The pinned server reads secret settings through documented source-level NAME_FILE support and rejects simultaneous NAME and NAME_FILE inputs. ADMIN_TOKEN may contain an Argon2id PHC hash, but enabling server administration is separate from creating or unlocking a vault account; keep it disabled unless explicitly needed.

The shared recipe generates one owner-only master-password file but does not bind it into the server or enable ADMIN_TOKEN. Vault account registration requires the Bitwarden client's KDF, authentication hash and wrapped encryption key; a generic email/password POST or an admin login is not a compatible first-owner bootstrap.

Applied private HTTPS and a stable canonical DOMAIN are prerequisites, not first-owner evidence. Shared setup still needs a separately pinned official-client enrollment and decrypted-unlock boundary. Keep the existing standalone signup/closure/recovery gate until that boundary exists; server health, a password-grant token, or an ADMIN_TOKEN session must never satisfy vault-account readiness.
security: Require a verified private HTTPS origin before account creation or client use; keep administration private, registration closed outside a bounded first-account gate, and recovery material protected.
Do not treat the shared loopback HTTP origin or a healthy container as web-vault acceptance.

apps.name: Vector
pitfalls: Broad Docker or host log access can collect unintended sensitive content.
The self-only recipe does not collect host or application logs; a running process or healthy API does not establish real ingestion.
security: Redact credentials and personal data before routing telemetry.
The unauthenticated observability API must remain on loopback or another private trusted network when enabled.

apps.name: VictoriaMetrics
pitfalls: Prometheus compatibility does not make retention and scaling choices identical.
security: Keep ingestion and query endpoints private unless authenticated.

apps.name: What's Up Docker
pitfalls: An available tag is not proof that an upgrade is compatible, backed up, or reversible.

Pinned 9.1.0 registerWatchers creates a default local Docker watcher when none is configured. Available watcher providers are Docker, Kubernetes, Nomad, and Swarm; registry providers look up image updates for watcher-supplied inventory and do not offer a standalone registry-only mode. A web-only Compose container without an approved watcher would not perform useful monitoring.
Do not expose raw Docker TCP port 2375 publicly or treat Docker socket :ro as an API permission boundary.
security: Do not mount the Docker socket directly; a read-only bind mount does not make Docker API operations read-only. Upstream recommends a Docker socket proxy with CONTAINERS, IMAGES, INFO, VERSION, EVENTS, and PING reads enabled and mutating operations denied. The proxy requires separate exact socket approval and a WUD-only network; never publish its Docker API port by default.

Keep the web UI private, seed WUD_AUTH_ADMIN_USER and WUD_AUTH_ADMIN_PASSWORD at the narrow apply boundary, and persist WUD state. Do not put the bootstrap password in catalog data or an ordinary report.

Pinned authenticated POST /api/profile/tokens accepts name and read scopes and returns rawSecret only once; inventory cannot recover it. Any future adapter must checkpoint before creation, save privately, and refuse duplicate creation after an uncertain response. Bearer verification also updates token lastUsedAt and needs an explicit mutation approval.

WUD_AUTH_ADMIN_USER with PASSWORD or HASH updates the matching user's credentials and administrator role on startup. Plan this as ongoing declarative credential ownership, not an empty-database-only seed. Homarr's pinned native WUD client uses saved Basic username/password on /api/containers; a personal token is not required for that client.

apps.name: ZeroTier
pitfalls: Virtual LAN reachability can expose services beyond their host bind assumptions.
A successful join or running container is not network acceptance. Verify listnetworks reports OK and an assigned address after controller authorization, then test peer reachability.
Persist /var/lib/zerotier-one across upgrades to preserve node identity; keep identity.secret and authtoken.secret private.

The userspace libzt sockets SDK requires application integration and is not a drop-in unprivileged network sidecar for arbitrary shared services. The localhost service API token and the owner's Central authorization token are separate credentials.

The recipe creates no networks and joins none. Native identity and controller API readback is bootstrap readiness only; controller choice, network creation, membership authorization, assigned addresses and peer routes remain pending.

The owner-volume retains identity and controller data. Resume requires the same saved token and node identity; unknown or changed ownership must be inspected, not reset. UPnP/NAT-PMP mapping and in-container software updates are disabled.
security: Review network membership, routes, and controller ownership before joining; a network ID alone does not authorize a node.

The pinned official image needs NET_ADMIN and /dev/net/tun through the source-bound tun-net-admin approval. It uses its own bridge namespace, not host networking, and does not grant host or sibling-service routing.

The native management token is generated once into the owner-private file and supplied through the documented ZEROTIER_API_SECRET environment. Docker operators can inspect this token; it is not a local admin password or a Central API credential.
